title: Mistakes were made at fatal standoff, inquiry told
article: The man who led a tactical team that tried to control a standoff with a mentally ill man told a fatality inquiry there were a number of mistakes made that day.
The standoff in Feb. 28, 2004 led to the death of suspect Martin Ostopovich and RCMP officer Cpl. Jim Galloway.

"We tried our best to deal with Mr. Ostopovich in a safe way. I tried to bring all my members home safely. You keep replaying this thing in my head," Randy Pearson, who has since retired from the RCMP, said. "When it's all said and done, I hope people realize we did our best."
Officers were called to Martin Ostopovich's Spruce Grove neighbourhood because someone reported what they thought was a bullet hole in a car window.

The 41-year-old Ostopovich was delusional and his wife warned police he was armed. When he tried to leave the home with two rifles, after an hours-long standoff, officers rammed his car to prevent him from fleeing.
Galloway, who wasn't a member of the tactical team but had volunteered to drive the ramming SUV, was shot and killed when he tried to take cover behind his vehicle.
Ostopovich was shot and killed by police.

Pearson said in retrospect, the plan to ram Ostopovich's car put Galloway directly in his line of sight, and he should have had Galloway stay in the vehicle. The other officer in the SUV, Cpl. Tim Taniguchi, ducked under the dash when he saw Ostopovich point a gun at him.
"Ramming that vehicle was a last resort, it is not something we wanted to do," Pearson said. "It is something we had to do, because if he left that cul-de-sac, who know what could happen.
"And it's my job to make sure innocent civilians are not in danger."
As well, he would have had Galloway ram the vehicle at a different angle, so he wouldn't have been directly in Ostopovich's way.
And he said he only realized he didn't have an ambulance standing by once he saw Galloway go down.
The families of Galloway and Ostopovich cried as Pearson testified.
The RCMP needs to provide better protective gear, Pearson said, because Galloway was wearing a bullet proof vest that was ineffective against the calibre of weapon Ostopovich was using.

Pearson broke RCMP rules and purchased better gear for his tactical team after the shootings, he said, adding most RCMP emergency response teams in Canada still don't have vests that protect against rifle fire.

"I hope that as a result of my testimony, senior management of the RCMP will pay more attention to this program and perhaps support it a little better than I think it has been supported, and equipment issues will be addressed," he said.
